claims.text: Adding approximately 1–3 wt% Y2O3 nanoparticles to a refractory W-Ta-Nb-Mo-V-based high-entropy alloy will improve its radiation tolerance.
The Y2O3 addition will not degrade mechanical integrity.
The Y2O3 addition will not compromise processing practicality.
Ball milling pre-alloyed powders followed by hot isostatic pressing can produce a uniform dispersion of Y2O3 nanoparticles in the alloy.
The introduced nanoparticles will remain well embedded in the refractory high-entropy-alloy matrix.
Dispersed Y2O3 nanoparticles provide preferential sites for annihilation of irradiation-induced defects.
Y2O3 nanoparticles pin grain boundaries and stabilize the alloy microstructure during irradiation.
Y2O3 nanoparticles capture and immobilize irradiation-generated vacancies.
Y2O3 nanoparticles capture and immobilize irradiation-generated interstitials.
Defect capture by the nanoparticles reduces the accumulation of dislocation loops and voids.
Reduced accumulation of dislocation loops and voids reduces irradiation-induced swelling and embrittlement.
The Y2O3 nanoparticles will form coherent interfaces with the matrix.
Coherent nanoparticle-matrix interfaces will provide dispersion strengthening.
The Y2O3-dispersed alloy will exhibit less irradiation-induced swelling than an otherwise comparable alloy without Y2O3.
The Y2O3-dispersed alloy will exhibit a lower post-irradiation defect density than the unmodified control.
The Y2O3-dispersed alloy will maintain or slightly increase yield strength relative to the irradiated control.
The Y2O3-dispersed alloy will maintain or slightly improve ductility relative to the irradiated control.
The proposed benefits are expected to hold around 500°C and within irradiation dose or flux ranges relevant to plasma-facing components.
The defect-sink mechanism of Y2O3 is supported in other high-temperature alloy systems.
